boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Devil's Backbone (Backbone Mountain) record (September 1, 1863) in Operations to Control Indian Territory [June-September 1863]. The Perryville raid (August 25-26), the August 31 skirmishes near Scullyville and the Poteau, and the occupation of Fort Smith are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 2nd Kansas Cavalry, 6th Missouri Cavalry, and two sections of Rabb's 2nd Indiana Battery [US] and Cabell's Brigade [CS], with no numerical bounds; the live field reads zero. Cabell says his brigade's aggregate was over 3,000 but he never had more than 1,600 in the field or 1,200 for duty, that desertion had reduced it to about 1,250 by August 31, that the enemy had at least 2,300 effective men and eight guns, and that Cloud pursued with 1,500 cavalry, six guns and 40 wagons of infantry; after the action he could raise no more than 900. Britton names Cloud's units as the Second Kansas and Sixth Missouri State Militia Cavalry and two sections of Rabb's battery, and Cabell's as three regiments and three battalions of cavalry, a regiment of infantry and a battery.
claims.rationale: An interested commander's aggregate, field and duty figures at different dates and his estimates of the enemy. Britton's 'State Militia' differs from the frozen unit name. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Britton says the country was rough and mountainous, with timber and brush at the foot of the mountain where a large force could lie near the road unseen. Cabell says he formed at the foot of Backbone Mountain about 16 miles from Fort Smith, with Monroe's regiment in ambush and the other regiments in echelon on the mountainside and the battery commanding the field.
claims.rationale: Ground from a history and an interested report; no map inspected. The ambush position was chosen by Cabell during the retreat.

Cabell says he placed Monroe's regiment in ambush and that several regiments and a battalion ran from the field. The frozen commanders are Brigadier General W. L. Cabell and Colonel William F. Cloud.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory and the live result Union Victory. Cabell says the enemy was repulsed and he withdrew in good order to Waldron after posting a picket on the field. Britton says a battalion and three of Cabell's regiments broke and ran, and Cloud occupied the field; NPS says the Confederates retired in disorder to Waldron.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Cabell's account of a repulse conflicts with the others.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 81 total (US 16; CS 65); the live field reads 31 (US 14; CS 17). Cabell gives his loss as 5 killed and 12 wounded with missing unknown, 6 killed and 14 wounded over two days, and claims the enemy lost about 30 killed and 100 to 150 wounded; he says a fleeing regiment carried off 80 prisoners under sentence from his provost guard. Britton repeats Cabell's 5 and 12 and gives Cloud's report of two killed, including Captain Lines, twelve wounded and thirty prisoners taken.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Cabell's Union figures are an interested claim; the released provost prisoners are not battle casualties.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam's, 1899) is a retrospective history described on its title page as based upon official reports and the author's observations; it relays figures from Union and Confederate reports, so it is not independent of the Official Records families, and is treated as partly a participant's interested Union account. Williams's July 1863 report on Cabin Creek, Cooper's August 12, 1863 report on Elk Creek (Honey Springs) and Cabell's December 7, 1863 report including Backbone Mountain are separate author families of interested accounts; Cooper's inclosed general orders are part of his report. Official Records Series I, Volume XXII, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
